reviewedBy: Claude Code, scheduled morning run, second firing, 11 November 2026
urgency: None. Held until the full text has been read.
reviewBasis: The abstract only, read in this run in two places that agree: the PubMed record 43000569 and the abstract the publisher deposited with Crossref for DOI 10.1007/s00431-026-07569-z. The full text was not read. Crossref lists the article under a Creative Commons licence, so it is open, but the Springer article page and PDF both answered the container with a browser challenge page, and the fetch tool was turned away for want of cookies. No figure is cleared from an abstract alone.

claims.claim: Once family circumstances are accounted for, children in single parent households do not have measurably different screen time.
claims.basis: Abstract: after full adjustment the association was not statistically significant, in the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children, ages 6 to 13, 8,706 children at baseline. Qualified because only the abstract was read, a result that is not significant is not proof of no difference, and how screen time was measured and who reported it is not in the abstract.

claims.claim: A child moving between a two parent and a single parent household does not change their screen time.
claims.basis: Abstract: neither direction of transition was associated with a change, using matched comparison children. The confidence intervals printed in the abstract are very wide, which says the number of children who made a transition was small. The honest reading is that no change was detected, not that there is none.

claims.claim: Each extra sibling goes with less screen time.
claims.basis: Abstract: an association of roughly twenty minutes a week less for each additional sibling. Small beside a week of screen time, observational, and the abstract does not say why. Not read in the full text.

claims.claim: The analysis was planned in advance.
claims.basis: The abstract calls the models pre registered. The registration itself was not found or read in this run.

claims.claim: Single parents can stop worrying about screens, or having brothers and sisters protects a child from screens.
claims.basis: Neither is in the abstract. The study measures amount of time, not what the time was spent on or what it did, and the sibling result is an association.

notQuotable: every figure in the abstract, including the sample size, the minutes per week and the confidence intervals: the full text was not read and nothing is cleared
any statement that family breakdown does or does not affect a child on screens
any statement that siblings reduce screen time as cause and effect
any carrying of the result across to UK families
evidenceConfidence: MODERATE that the abstract says what is written here: it was read in two independent records that agree. NOT ASSESSED as evidence, because the methods, the measure of screen time and the limitations are in a full text that could not be reached.
limitations: Abstract only. The methods, results tables and the authors own limitations were not read.
Australian children. Nothing on the UK.
How screen time was measured, and whether a parent or the child reported it, is not stated in the abstract.
The confidence intervals for the two transition results are very wide, so the study could not rule out changes of an hour or more a week in either direction.
It measures amount of screen time only. Nothing on content, context or what a family does together.
Ages 6 to 13. Nothing on older teenagers.
Observational, even with matching. Unmeasured differences between families remain possible.
contradictoryEvidence: From the same abstract: the authors open by saying children screen time does vary by family structure in earlier cross sectional work. Their finding is that the difference is largely explained by sociodemographic factors, which is not the same as there being no difference in what families live with.
From the same abstract: the transition estimates point in opposite directions with intervals that span zero widely, so they do not agree with each other on anything beyond no detectable change.
The earlier cross sectional studies the abstract refers to were not read in this run.
whatThisDoesNotProve: That family structure has no effect on a child digital life.
That more siblings cause less screen time.
Anything about harm, benefit, or what children do on screens.
Anything about what a parent should do.
mediaMisrepresentation: Coverage was not searched in this run.
gdcBeliefs: Evidence or silence. An abstract is a pointer, not a source.
It neither flatters nor cuts against what we sell. Its use to us would be to keep blame off single parents, and that needs the full text first.
unresolvedQuestions: The full text. It is open access, so the PDF can be left in Drive and ingested with ingest.mjs, after which this review is redone from the paper.
How many children made each transition.
